On 11/30/2014 01:36 PM, Michael Laakasuo wrote:
> I did. I found the problem. The term that is missing is F1 =~ c(0, NA)*ITEM1
> However, this term is in my model, but it is dropped from the fitted
> model. Although this same term WORKS in the baselinemodel, it is only
> dropped when I add the groups.equal = "loadings" that this is dropped.
>
> How do I fix this?

You can use the group.partial= argument, to free up a factor loading.
But for 'custom' equality constraints, I would avoid the
convenient-but-global group.equal= argument, and use labels. So, 'equal'
factor loadings get the same label, as in

F1 =~ c(l1, l1)*ITEM1

while those that are allowed to be free get a different label:

F1 =~ c(l1, l2)*ITEM1

If, in addition, you need to fix 'l1' to zero, while 'l2' should be
free, you can write

F =~ c(l1, l2)*ITEM1 + c(0, NA)*ITEM1

Yves.

> Unlike Mplus, lavaan does not handle constraints with a 0 on the left

Hm. lavaan can handle this perfectly well. But lavaan (0.5-17) does not
like to have fixed parameters in the "==" formula. The 'lam1' parameter
is fixed (to 1) by default.

In the Mplus syntax, this parameter is explicitly made free:

f2 by LOT1* (lam1)

So you can the same in lavaan, by writing

f2 =~ NA*x1 + lam1*x1 + lam2*x2 + lam3*x3 + lam4*x4 + lam5*x5 + lam6*x6

+ lam7*x7 + lam8*x8 + lam9*x9

or use std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE

Yves.

I see these lines of syntax:

groundhydro=~GWDI+HWTE

phaseloc=~HWTE

HWTE~~0*HWTE

phaseloc~groundhydro+morphodist+habitatcond

This says that HWTE is an observed variable indicator for both groundhydro and phaseloc, and the residual variance of HWTE is 0.  One way to interpret this is that you have transformed the residual of HWTE from its relationship with groundhydro into the factor phaseloc.  Then you use groundhydro, the explained part of HWTE, to predict the transformed residual, phaseloc.  I would expect the relationship to be poor, as indeed the results suggest.

To establish phaseloc as something other than the residual of HWTE, phaseloc needs another indicator, or else you need to constrain the loading of HWTE on groundhydro, so that you specify how much of HWTE’s explained variance is due to groundhydro and how much is left for phaseloc.

In general, yes, you can find an indicator performing very poorly.  The very fact that of being surprised suggests that you need to go back and rethink, unless there is some error in the syntax..

--Ed Rigdon

Jonas—

     That’s actually about it.  You will square the indicators, and out of that extract a variance component that corresponds to the square of the factor.  The indProd function in the semTools package does a nice job.  Specify the set of three indicators for both the first set and the second set, and set match=T.  When you run the lavaan analysis, choose estimator=”MLR” because of the nonnormality of the products.

     You read more about factor interactions than about quadratics, but the two track along side by side.  The most sophisticated approaches—Klein and Moosbrugger’s (2000) LMS method and Muthen’s QML/random slope approximation to LMS--do not square indicators, but they are not available in R yet, to my knowledge.  Often, though, the differences across methods are inconsequential.

--Ed Rigdon

messages.body_plain:
Hello.  In order to show students what happens when one fits a model that is underidentified, I generated data from a simple measurement model with one "latent" and four "observed" variables and then fit the model without fixing either the variance of the latent or any of the path coefficients.  I expected that lavaan would tell me that there were convergence problems or some other type of error message.  However, when I fit the model to the data, lavaan reports a normal convergence and even prints out a ML chi-square value and a null probability.  The only sign of a problem is that it can't calculate the SE of the parameters.  The degrees of freedom (1) show that neither the latent variance nor any of the path coefficients were fixed and the parTable() function (reproduced below) shows that all of the parameters were free.
Why (and how...) can lavaan converge and estimate values for these free parameters when the model is underidentified?  Why doesn't it print out a warning about underidentification?

Michael—

     Fixing residual variances makes the single indicator factor models identified.  Also remember that the lavaan:::sem function has defaults.  If you run the same model using lavaan:::lavaan, it may fail the identification check.  The parTable function might clarify exactly which parameters were estimated under each different specification.

     Observed variable predictors may be modeled either as random variables with random sampling error or as “fixed-x” variables.  If treated as “fixed-x,” the rules change substantially.  Ask for residuals and the model-implied covariance matrix to see the difference.  A variable cannot be “fixed-x” if it is dependent, so treating those variables as indicators of factor achieved the same thing as “fixed.x=F”, and fixing residual variances at 0 made factor and indicator identical.

--Ed Rigdon

On 12/05/2014 10:25 PM, Bill Shipley wrote:
> Why (and how...) can lavaan converge and estimate values for these free
> parameters when the model is underidentified?  Why doesn't it print out
> a warning about underidentification?

Well, this seems not so strange to me.

Why do you still get estimates? Well, if a model is underidentified,
lavaan (or any other program for that matter) can usually still come up
with good estimates anyway (and some people exploit this 'feature'). The
solution, of course, may not be unique. If this is problematic, depends
on the setting.

Why 'convergence'? The optimizer has no idea if a model is identified or
not. It simply tries to minimize a discrepancy function. And it may very
well find a local minimum.

Why not a warning? Well, not getting standard errors is already a big
warning that something is wrong. Although this is not always due to
underidentification. Nevertheless, lavaan 0.5-17 does print:

"lavaan NOTE: this may be a symptom that the model is not identified"

The more interesting question is: can lavaan not detect this from just
scanning the parameter table? Perhaps, but it is not trivial. Just
following some rules of thumb is not enough. For example, for the
1-factor example, lavaan could check if either a factor loading was
fixed to a constant, or if the variance of the factor was fixed. But
suppose we use effect coding to fix the metric of the latent variable, as in

f =~ NA*x1 + a*x1 + b*x2 + c*x3 + d*x4
f ~~ f # free
a + b + c + d == 4

we may falsely flag this model as underidentified. In short, determining
if a model is underidentified just by scanning the parameter table is
rather difficult.

Yves.

In semTools::moreFitIndices(), we use a hidden function semTools:::sic() to calculate the stochastic information criterion (SIC).  The calculation requires the the determinant of the information matrix, which we retrieve using

> solve(vcov(fit))

I just tried this for the first time on a model with equality constraints for factor loadings, and it returns an error because the vcov(fit) has redundant parameter estimates along the diagonal that are perfectly correlated (e.g., visual=~x1 is perfectly correlated with visual=~x1.g2, etc.). > visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
> textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
> speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
> visual ~~ c(1, NA)*visual

>                   group = "school", group.equal = "loadings")
> moreFitIndices(fit.metric)

Since SEs are returned when there are equality constraints, I assume you have found a way to work around this issue by working with a Hessian or information matrix that excludes redundant parameters.  I was hoping you could provide a suggestion for a solution, or perhaps somewhere to look in your source code so I can get an idea of what you do behind the scenes. This is called "matching"--multiplying the first indicator of A times the first indicator of B, the second by the second, the third by the third, etc.  Formally, it was "the best times the best, the second best times the second best . . ". The motivation to do this, rather than multiply all times all, is to limit the nonnormality in the model.  Each product term will be nonnormal, even if the original indicators were normal. Ed is right on describing the matched pair strategy, but it should be used with caution. While including only matched pair limits non-normality in the model, it makes a (fairly strong) assumption of tau equivalence (all indicators of a latent variable have equal factor loadings). I am afraid you need the full data to compute this matrix. It is the the
diagonal of a weight matrix which is based on an estimate of the
asymptotic variance matrix of all sample statistics (thresholds,
correlations, etc).

DWLS. You can use ULS.

Yves.

F2 =~ x4 + x5 + x6
F1.F2 =~ x1.x4 + x1.x5 + x1.x6 + x2.x4 + x2.x5 + x2.x6 + x3.x4 + x3.x5 + x3.x6

x2.x5 ~~ x3.x5
x2.x6 ~~ x3.x6
x3.x4 ~~ x3.x5
x3.x4 ~~ x3.x6

On 12/11/2014 01:36 AM, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> Hi Yves,
>
> In semTools::moreFitIndices(), we use a hidden function
> semTools:::sic() to calculate the stochastic information criterion
> (SIC).  The calculation requires the the determinant of the information
> matrix, which we retrieve using
>
>     solve(vcov(fit))
>
>
> I just tried this for the first time on a model with equality
> constraints for factor loadings, and it returns an error because
> thevcov(fit) has redundant parameter estimates

Hi Terry,

This is a tricky one. Because the way lavaan is handling this
internally, has changed (between 0.5-17 and 0.5-18, which is still under
development).

I will give you an explanation (of how we 'invert' the information
matrix in the presence of equality constraints to get vcov) for 0.5-18
(but let me know if you need the info for 0.5-17 too). At least for the
se="standard" setting.

In 0.5-18, all equality constraints are handled using a 'constraint'
function. For your example, it is in

fit.metric@Mod...@ceq.function

This function evaluates the constraints, and returns all zeroes if all
constraints are satisfied. The Jacobian (first derivative) of this
function is called 'R', and can be caculated as

R <- lav_func_jacobian_complex(func = fit.metric@Mod...@ceq.function, x =
fit.metric@Fit@x)

which has size '9 x 63'. The columns are the 'free' (but unconstrained)
model parameters.

Now, the information matrix will have size 63 x 63, but will be singular
(in your case, rank = 60)

# for se="standard"
E <- lavaan:::computeExpectedInformation(fit.metric@Model,
lavsamplestats = fit.metric@SampleStats)
qr(E)$rank

To get the inverse of E (to compute standard errors), we can not simply
invert E. But, we can invert the so-called bordered information matrix:

Z <- rbind( cbind(E, t(R)), cbind(R, matrix(0,nrow(R),nrow(R))) )

and then take the upper-left 63 x 63 block:

E.inv <- solve(Z)[1:63, 1:63]

This 'trick' dates back to (at least) Aitchison and Silvey (1958).
The SE's are then

sqrt(diag(E.inv/301))

What I will try to do is to provide an inspect(fit, "information"), and
maybe an inspect(fit, "information.inverse"), to return the proper
(possibly singular) information matrix (or its inverse), depending on
the 'se=' argument.

Now, I am not sure about the determinant. I am not familiar with 'sic',
but my guess would be that you need the determinant of the
'non-redundant' information matrix. To get this one, you can compute the
null space of R:

QR <- qr(t(R))
ranK <- QR$rank
Q <- qr.Q(QR, complete = TRUE)
Q1 <- Q[,1:ranK, drop = FALSE]         # range space
Q2 <- Q[,-seq_len(ranK), drop = FALSE] # null space

The Q2 matrix will be '63 x 54' matrix and can be used to 'project' E to
the 54 x 54 (nonredundant) subspace:

E2 <- t(Q2) %*% E %*% Q2

and this should give you a non-singular matrix, and hence you can get a
determinant:

det(E2)

Hope this helps,

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Eiko,

(1 & 2)

Robust estimators are not applied to point estimates, just to SE estimates and the chi-square test statistic.  In other words, the first step in MLR is to just run regular ML to get the point estimates (which is what you see in the summary() output), then the data's characteristics are used to adjust the usual SE/fit estimates so they have closer-to-nominal performance.  Using MLR, the left column is the regular fit statistic you would see if you just used estimator = "ML", and the right column is after the robust corrections are applied (i.e., the only output you see in Mplus when using MLR).  Same with WLSMV: the left column is using DWLS with no robust corrections for the fit statistic, and the right column is after applying the robust correction (so the right column is the one you want to pay attention to, even if it's bad news).  Here is a great paper explaining these and other robust corrections in SEM:

http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2013.824793

I think Yves has answered this question before, and provided a different source article for DWLS and robust differences, so try searching "DWLS robust" keywords at the top of the lavaan Google Group page.

(3)

You can get R-squared for any outcomes (e.g., observed indicators, endogenous latent factors) by requesting it in the summary(), or using the inspect() function:

> summary(fit, rsquare = TRUE)
> inspect(fit, "rsquare")

(4)

I'm not sure how long you mean by "forever", but Mplus will generally be faster than lavaan because lavaan is written completely in R (not a programming language like C or Fortran).  It might take especially long if you have a large sample size, lots of missing data, or other things that make a model take a bit more time to converge.

semTools currently only has functions measurementInvariance (across groups for continuous indicators), measurementInvarianceCat (across groups for ordinal indicators), and longInvariance (across time, and potentially groups as well, for continuous indicators of only a single factor).  There is room for further development in all of these functions, but for right now, you'll just need to specify your few models and run them manually to test longitudinal invariance with ordinal indicators.

Terry

messages.body_plain:
Presumably you're getting an error/warning?

MLR is used to estimate standard errors under non-normality.

Bootstrap is used to estimate standard errors using the parameter estimates. The parameter estimates for MLR are the same as ML, so there's no point bootstrapping MLR estimates.

(How do you know your latent variable is not normal?)

Jeremy
